item.title: Architecture
item.description:
Functional requirements

  • Runs entirely client-side, including from file:// — no server, no install, no build step.
  • Loads data as plain .js files injected via <script> tags (not fetch(), which file:// blocks), writing into a shared window.DS namespace.

Key decisions

  • No bundler, no framework. Each module is a small UMD-style IIFE attaching to window.DS_APP in the browser and exporting via module.exports under Node for tests — see util.js’s el() hyperscript helper for the lowest layer.
  • A single store + reducer (store.js), split into one reducer per action-namespace domain (preset/*, group/*, table/*, …), dispatched through a small pub/sub (createStore).
  • A lazy columnar source format: each source file defines one function per field, returning that field’s values for every row positionally — V8 never materializes a field’s function body unless it’s actually called, so unused fields cost nothing to load.
  • Formulas, not eval. Computed fields use a small hand-written tokenizer/parser/evaluator (formula.js), deliberately not eval/new Function, since presets are plain JSON files people exchange.

Testing

Pure-function modules (dataset.js, entities.js, formula.js, export.js, store.js) are the reason this architecture keeps a hard line between logic and DOM-touching code: it’s what makes them cleanly covered by node:test unit tests in the first place. See Testing for how to actually run the suite.

item.title: Join two sources
item.description:
Task: you have a CRM export (customers) and an ERP export (prices and stock), and want one table with both.

  1. On Data, check both sources.
  2. A join row appears for the second source. Pick the join type (LEFT to keep every CRM row even without an ERP match is usually the right default) and the matching field on each side (e.g. customer_id ↔ client_ref).
  3. Check the fields you want from each source.
  4. Open Table — the result has one row per matched (or unmatched, for LEFT/RIGHT/FULL) pair.

(More recipes — conditions, formulas, grouping with aggregates — coming soon.)

item.title: Screens
item.description:
JoinSheets has three screens, reached from the top nav.

Data

Sources, joins between them, and conditions on raw fields — what comes after FROM/WHERE in SQL. Pick which sources and fields to use, then join them (left/right/inner/full) if there’s more than one.

Fields

What comes after SELECT: which columns the result table has, and how they’re computed — a field as-is, a renamed/typed field, collision resolution between several inputs by weight, or a formula.

item.title: Testing
item.description:
JoinSheets has no build step, no bundler, and no CI – which means nothing runs your tests for you automatically. Running them yourself, before opening a pull request, is the whole safety net. This page covers what’s there and how to run it.

Unit tests

Plain node:test (Node’s built-in test runner – no test framework dependency), under tests/. Run the whole suite with:

./run_tests.sh

(a thin wrapper around node --test tests/*.test.js – an explicit file list, not a recursive search, so the optional import/ submodule’s own tests don’t get swept into this repository’s run).

item.title: Releases
item.description:
This section describes the core principles behind JoinSheets’ release policy and the workflow for shipping a new release.

Development phase

The project is currently in beta: the core functionality is settled, and work now is about polishing individual pieces based on what early users run into.

During alpha, changes landed fast and somewhat chaotically, as new ideas or different ways to implement a feature came up, and releases were spontaneous – driven by how fast development was moving and how much had changed.

item.title: Contributing
item.description:
JoinSheets is under active development, and any engagement is genuinely appreciated – an issue, a pull request, feedback on any platform, even a star on GitHub.

For users

The team is actively working on usability and the interface, and makes changes based on real user experience. The best contribution from a user is an issue: report whatever got in your way or felt inconvenient. Include the app’s version – right now that means checking <meta name="version"> in the page source (View Page Source, or your browser’s dev tools); there’s no in-app display of it yet.
